::: {.puzzle}
A harmonica reed is a little brass bar, fixed at one end and free at the other, like a kalimba tine, with the same overtones, in the ideal model, at 6.27 and 17.55 times its fundamental. Pluck it and you hear them. Blow it and they are gone: every frequency in the note lands exactly on the whole-number lines. Where did they go?
:::

Pluck the reed, then blow it, and compare the stems with the gray whole-number lines.

::: {.gist}
**The gist.** A steadily blown note does not contain the reed's overtones at their own frequencies. The reed becomes a valve that chops the airflow into puffs, and you hear mainly the puffs. A steadily blown reed settles into one motion that repeats exactly, so the puffs repeat too, and a sound that repeats has frequencies only on the whole-number lines. The reed's own overtones decide what a pluck sounds like; the repeating airflow decides what a blown note sounds like.
:::

## On the pitch ruler

Plucked, the reed's overtones sit at 6.27× and 17.55×, off the gray lines, and die almost at once, as on the kalimba. Blown, the stems sit at 1×, 2×, 3×, 4×, …, every one on a line. Each stem's height is how strong that frequency is in the sound. Same reed; only the way it is played differs.

## How it works

**The same bar as a kalimba tine.** A reed is riveted at one end and free at the other, so everything worked out on the [kalimba page](kalimba.qmd) applies unchanged: its modes sit at 1, 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest. Low reeds are long, high reeds are short. The reed's width does not change its pitch, only how much air it moves.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The reed's operator and its lowest frequency <span class="needs">uses partial derivatives</span></summary>

A reed is riveted at one end and free at the other, so the equation, operator and end conditions of the kalimba page apply unchanged:
$$
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx}, \qquad u = u_x = 0 \text{ at the rivet}, \qquad u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \text{ at the tip}.
$$
The mode frequencies are in the ratios $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$. For a rectangular reed of width $w$ and thickness $h$, $I = wh^3/12$ and the cross-section area is $S = wh$, so $\kappa^2 = EI/(\rho S) = Eh^2/(12\rho)$. With $\beta_1 = 1.8751/L$ and $\omega = \kappa\beta^2$ from the kalimba page, the lowest frequency $f_1 = \omega_1/2\pi$ is
$$
f_1 = \frac{(1.8751)^2}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{h}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{E}{12\rho}} .
$$
The width $w$ cancels, so it affects how much air the reed moves, not its pitch.

</details>
:::

**Blowing turns the reed into a valve.** Blow, and the reed swings through its slot, opening and closing the air path hundreds of times a second. The sound comes mainly from the chopped airflow; the acoustics writer Colin Pykett notes that very little comes from the reed's own motion. A steadily blown reed settles into a motion that repeats itself exactly, at a playing frequency slightly below its first mode's, so the puffs of air repeat at that rate too. A sound that repeats has frequencies only at whole-number multiples of its repetition rate ([page 0](note.qmd)). So the blown note lands on the lines, with strong odd and even multiples (Pykett), even though the reed's own overtones do not. Why the reed locks into one repeating motion is observed, and reproduced by computer models of reeds, but not derived here; the fold gives a plausible picture.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>Why a steady train of puffs has only whole-number partials <span class="needs">uses Fourier series (page 3)</span></summary>

Let $q(t)$ be the airflow through the slot. Once the blown reed has settled into its steady oscillation, the opening, and so $q$, repeats every $P = 1/f_p$ seconds: $q(t + P) = q(t)$. A steady oscillation kept going by a steady push, like this one, is called a [self-sustained oscillation](glossary.qmd#self-sustained), and the repeating cycle it settles into a *limit cycle*; the bowed string and the clarinet reed are others. That it settles into one is observed, and reproduced by nonlinear models of reeds; it is not derived here. A plausible picture, not a derivation: the airflow feeds energy mainly into the first mode, the other modes are not kept going at their own frequencies, and in the repeating cycle they move only as they are pushed, at whole-number multiples of $f_p$. By the [circle page](circle.qmd), a periodic function of period $P$ is a Fourier series in $\cos(2\pi nt/P)$ and $\sin(2\pi nt/P)$, so it contains only the frequencies $n f_p$. How strong each one is depends on the shape of a single puff: short, sharp puffs give strong high partials. The argument uses only that the motion repeats, not which modes make it up, which is why the reed's own overtone frequencies, 6.27 and 17.55 times $f_1$, do not appear.

The demo's sound is a model: one puff shape, chosen so that the open part of each cycle is short, repeated at the playing frequency, then passed through two broad peaks, a stand-in for resonances of the player's mouth and the instrument. The peaks were set by ear, not measured, so the timbre is approximate. The pitch and the whole-number spacing are not approximations.

</details>
:::

The same mechanism drives the bowed string and the clarinet: a steady push, from the bow or the breath, turned into a sound that repeats. On those instruments the string's or tube's own frequencies already sit nearly on the lines, so the push and the instrument agree, and locking is easy. A free reed's own frequencies are far off the lines, which lets you hear that the way it is driven, not the reed's own frequencies, decides where a blown note's overtones sit.

**Tuning a reed with a file.** Reed makers tune by scraping metal off, and where they scrape decides the direction. The first mode bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thin the reed near the rivet and you remove stiffness where it counts: the pitch drops. Thin it near the tip and you remove mass where it counts: the pitch rises. It is the spring of [page 1](oscillator.qmd) again, where frequency grows with stiffness and falls with mass. Try it below.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
    <div class="slider"><label for="fx">Where to file</label><input type="range" id="fx" min="0.02" max="0.98" step="0.01" value="0.1"><output id="fxo">base</output></div>
    <div class="readout" id="fRead"></div>
    <div class="controls"><button id="fPlay" class="primary">Blow the filed reed</button><button id="fOrig">Blow the original</button></div>
    <p class="cap">Filing removes a quarter of the thickness over about a tenth of the reed. The pitch change is estimated as in the fold below.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>Why filing moves the pitch: stiffness against mass <span class="needs">uses integration by parts and a first-order approximation</span></summary>

The [Rayleigh quotient](glossary.qmd#rayleigh-quotient) explains the direction. For the first mode,
$$
\omega_1^2 = \min_{u} \frac{\int_0^L EI\,(u'')^2\,dx}{\int_0^L \rho S\,u^2\,dx},
$$
the minimum taken over shapes, not identically zero, that satisfy the conditions at the rivet; the minimizing shape is the first mode itself. This is $\omega^2 = k/m$ from page 1 again: stiffness on top, weighted by where the reed bends, and mass at the bottom, weighted by where it moves. The first mode bends most near the rivet and moves most near the tip. Thinning the reed near the rivet removes stiffness where it counts and lowers the pitch; thinning it near the tip removes mass where it counts and raises it. The steps below make this quantitative.

1. *The quotient.* Multiply $\rho S\,\omega^2X = (EI\,X'')''$ by $X$ and integrate by parts twice; the boundary terms vanish at the rivet and at the free tip, as on the kalimba page. This gives $\omega^2 = \int EI(X'')^2 / \int \rho S X^2$ for every mode.
2. *Small change.* File the reed so that its thickness changes by $\delta h(x) < 0$. Then $I \propto h^3$ changes by $\delta(EI) = 3EI\,\delta h/h$, and $S \propto h$ changes by $\delta(\rho S) = \rho S\,\delta h/h$, to [first order](glossary.qmd#first-order), that is, ignoring terms in $(\delta h)^2$.
3. *First order.* Because the first mode minimizes the quotient, changing the shape slightly changes the quotient only by an amount proportional to the square of the change. So to first order one may keep the old mode shape $X$ and change only the coefficients:
$$
\delta(\omega^2) = \frac{\int \frac{\delta h}{h}\,\big(3EI\,(X'')^2 - \omega^2\rho S\,X^2\big)\,dx}{\int \rho S\,X^2\,dx}.
$$
4. *Sign.* Near the rivet $X \approx 0$ and $X''$ is largest, so the bracket is positive and, with $\delta h < 0$, $\omega$ drops. Near the tip $X'' = 0$ and $X$ is largest, so the bracket is negative and $\omega$ rises. In between there is a point where filing changes nothing, to first order.

The demo uses the full quotient with the original mode shape, which is accurate to first order in the depth of filing.

</details>
:::

**The chromatic slide.** A chromatic harmonica has two sets of reed chambers, the second tuned a [semitone](glossary.qmd#semitone) higher. Each hole has a blow reed, sounded by breathing out, and a [draw](glossary.qmd#draw) reed, sounded by breathing in, in each set. Pushing the slide moves a perforated bar that closes one set and opens the other, so every note rises a semitone. In *solo tuning*, the usual layout for a chromatic harmonica, each group of four holes holds C, E, G, C on the blow and D, F, A, B on the draw. Here is a whole one to play.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<section class="instrument" aria-labelledby="play">
  <div class="harp-legend"><span>blow, breathing out (top row: keys 1 … =)</span><span>draw, breathing in (bottom row: keys Q … ])</span></div>
  <div class="harp" id="harp" aria-label="Twelve-hole chromatic harmonica in C"></div>
  <div class="controls" style="padding:0.6rem 0.25rem 0">
    <button id="slide">Slide (hold, or Space)</button>
    <span class="readout" id="hRead">Press and hold a hole. Slide across holes to move between notes.</span>
  </div>
  <p class="cap" style="padding:0.4rem 0.25rem 0">Twelve holes in solo tuning (explained just above), from C4, middle C, up three octaves. Pushing the slide raises every note a semitone, by switching the air to a second set of reeds.</p>
</section>
</div>
```

## What we found

On the pitch ruler, the plucked reed's overtones are off the lines and die fast, like a kalimba's. Blown, the sound repeats, so every frequency in it sits on a line, and you hear a clean note. The operator decides which frequencies an object can vibrate at; the way it is driven decides what you hear.

::: {.family}
**Same operator as the kalimba.** Accordion, concertina and harmonium reeds are [free reeds](glossary.qmd#free-reed) too: they swing freely through a slot, unlike a clarinet's reed, which beats against the mouthpiece. All of them are cantilevers like the kalimba's tine: same operator, same ends, smaller and thinner, usually of brass in harmonicas and harmoniums and of steel in accordions and concertinas. What separates a harmonica from a kalimba is the excitation, steady airflow instead of one pluck.
:::

## The next puzzle

Piano tuners deliberately tune octaves a little wider than 2 : 1. Why would exact sound wrong?

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core;
  // solo tuning in C: [blow, draw] MIDI notes for holes 1..12
  var HOLES = [];
  for (var o = 0; o < 3; o++) {
    var c = 60 + 12 * o;
    HOLES.push([c, c + 2], [c + 4, c + 5], [c + 7, c + 9], [c + 12, c + 11]);
  }
  var BLOWC = ["Digit1", "Digit2", "Digit3", "Digit4", "Digit5", "Digit6", "Digit7", "Digit8", "Digit9", "Digit0", "Minus", "Equal"];
  var DRAWC = ["KeyQ", "KeyW", "KeyE", "KeyR", "KeyT", "KeyY", "KeyU", "KeyI", "KeyO", "KeyP", "BracketLeft", "BracketRight"];
  var slide = false, cur = null, voice = null, wave = null;
  var harp = document.getElementById("harp"), cells = [];
  function label(k) { return C.noteName(C.mtof(k)).name.replace(/\d+$/, ""); }
  HOLES.forEach(function (h, i) {
    var cell = document.createElement("div"); cell.className = "cell";
    var num = document.createElement("span"); num.className = "num"; num.textContent = i + 1;
    var b = document.createElement("button"); b.type = "button"; b.className = "blow"; b.dataset.hole = i; b.dataset.dir = 0;
    var d = document.createElement("button"); d.type = "button"; d.className = "draw"; d.dataset.hole = i; d.dataset.dir = 1;
    cell.appendChild(num); cell.appendChild(b); cell.appendChild(d); harp.appendChild(cell); cells.push([b, d]);
  });
  function relabel() { HOLES.forEach(function (h, i) { cells[i][0].textContent = label(h[0] + (slide ? 1 : 0)); cells[i][1].textContent = label(h[1] + (slide ? 1 : 0)); }); }
  function note(c) { return HOLES[c.hole][c.dir] + (slide ? 1 : 0); }
  function getWave(a) { if (!wave) wave = C.wave(a, C.models.harmonica.partials()); return wave; }
  // A harmonica voice: the reed's puff train (rich in odd and even harmonics), shaped by the resonances of the reed
  // chamber and the player's mouth, plus a little breath noise. The resonance and noise settings are by ear, not measured.
  var noiseBuf = null;
  function noise(a) {
    if (!noiseBuf) { noiseBuf = a.createBuffer(1, a.sampleRate * 2, a.sampleRate); var d = noiseBuf.getChannelData(0); for (var i = 0; i < d.length; i++) d[i] = Math.random() * 2 - 1; }
    var n = a.createBufferSource(); n.buffer = noiseBuf; n.loop = true; return n;
  }
  function sound(c) {
    var a = C.ac(), f = C.mtof(note(c)), t = a.currentTime;
    if (!voice) {
      var osc = a.createOscillator(), g = a.createGain(), out = a.createGain();
      osc.setPeriodicWave(getWave(a)); osc.frequency.value = f;
      var f1 = a.createBiquadFilter(); f1.type = "peaking"; f1.frequency.value = 1300; f1.Q.value = 1.4; f1.gain.value = 7;
      var f2 = a.createBiquadFilter(); f2.type = "peaking"; f2.frequency.value = 2900; f2.Q.value = 1.8; f2.gain.value = 5;
      var lp = a.createBiquadFilter(); lp.type = "lowpass"; lp.frequency.value = 7000; lp.Q.value = 0.5;
      var hp = a.createBiquadFilter(); hp.type = "highpass"; hp.frequency.value = 180;
      osc.connect(f1); f1.connect(f2); f2.connect(lp); lp.connect(hp); hp.connect(g);
      var nz = noise(a), nb = a.createBiquadFilter(), ng = a.createGain();
      nb.type = "bandpass"; nb.frequency.value = 2200; nb.Q.value = 0.8; ng.gain.value = 0.035;
      nz.connect(nb); nb.connect(ng); ng.connect(g);
      g.gain.setValueAtTime(0, t); g.gain.linearRampToValueAtTime(0.32, t + 0.025); g.gain.setTargetAtTime(0.26, t + 0.025, 0.08);
      g.connect(out); out.gain.value = 1; out.connect(C.out); osc.start(); nz.start();
      voice = { osc: osc, g: g, nz: nz };
    } else voice.osc.frequency.setTargetAtTime(f, t, 0.004);
    var nn = C.noteName(f);
    document.getElementById("hRead").innerHTML = "hole <b>" + (c.hole + 1) + "</b> " + (c.dir ? "draw" : "blow") + (slide ? " + slide" : "") + " · <b>" + nn.name + "</b> · " + f.toFixed(1) + " Hz";
  }
  function silence() { if (!voice) return; var t = C.ac().currentTime; voice.g.gain.cancelScheduledValues(t); voice.g.gain.setTargetAtTime(0, t, 0.03); voice.osc.stop(t + 0.3); voice.nz.stop(t + 0.3); voice = null; }
  function light(c, on) { if (c) cells[c.hole][c.dir].classList.toggle("on", on); }
  function set(c) { light(cur, false); cur = c; if (c) { light(c, true); sound(c); } else silence(); }
  function at(e) { var el = document.elementFromPoint(e.clientX, e.clientY); return el && el.dataset && el.dataset.hole != null ? { hole: +el.dataset.hole, dir: +el.dataset.dir } : null; }
  var down = false;
  harp.addEventListener("pointerdown", function (e) { e.preventDefault(); down = true; harp.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); set(at(e)); });
  harp.addEventListener("pointermove", function (e) { if (!down) return; var c = at(e); if (c && (!cur || c.hole !== cur.hole || c.dir !== cur.dir)) set(c); });
  function up() { down = false; set(null); }
  harp.addEventListener("pointerup", up); harp.addEventListener("pointercancel", up);
  function setSlide(on) { slide = on; document.getElementById("slide").classList.toggle("on", on); relabel(); if (cur) sound(cur); }
  var sb = document.getElementById("slide");
  sb.addEventListener("pointerdown", function (e) { e.preventDefault(); sb.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); setSlide(true); });
  sb.addEventListener("pointerup", function () { setSlide(false); }); sb.addEventListener("pointercancel", function () { setSlide(false); });
  var keyCell = {};
  // capture phase, so the page claims its keys before the blog's search shortcut sees them
  function mine(e) { return e.code === "Space" || BLOWC.indexOf(e.code) >= 0 || DRAWC.indexOf(e.code) >= 0; }
  window.addEventListener("keydown", function (e) {
    if (e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey || e.altKey || (e.target && e.target.tagName === "INPUT") || !mine(e)) return;
    e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation(); if (e.repeat) return;
    if (e.code === "Space") { setSlide(true); return; }
    var i = BLOWC.indexOf(e.code), dir = 0; if (i < 0) { i = DRAWC.indexOf(e.code); dir = 1; }
    keyCell[e.code] = true; set({ hole: i, dir: dir });
  }, true);
  window.addEventListener("keyup", function (e) {
    if (e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey || e.altKey || (e.target && e.target.tagName === "INPUT") || !mine(e)) return;
    e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation();
    if (e.code === "Space") { setSlide(false); return; }
    if (keyCell[e.code]) { delete keyCell[e.code]; set(null); }
  }, true);

  // plucked vs blown
  var mode = "blow";
  function hspec() {
    var p = C.models.harmonica.partials({ plucked: mode === "pluck" });
    C.stems(document.getElementById("hSpec"), p, { W: 320, H: 110, rmax: 20, fs: 8, sw: 2, labelEvery: 2 });
  }
  function fadeOut(b, s) { var d = b.getChannelData(0), n = Math.floor(s * b.sampleRate); for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) d[d.length - 1 - i] *= i / n; return b; }
  document.getElementById("pluckR").addEventListener("click", function () { mode = "pluck"; hspec(); C.play(C.render(C.toHz(C.models.harmonica.partials({ plucked: true }), 523.25), 2.0), 0.8); });
  document.getElementById("blowR").addEventListener("click", function () { mode = "blow"; hspec(); C.play(fadeOut(C.render(C.toHz(C.models.harmonica.partials(), 523.25), 1.6), 0.25), 0.6); });

  // reed filing
  var fx = document.getElementById("fx"), fxo = document.getElementById("fxo");
  function ratio() { return C.reedRatio(parseFloat(fx.value), 0.25, 0.06); }
  function fRead() {
    var x = parseFloat(fx.value), r = ratio(), cents = 1200 * Math.log2(r);
    fxo.textContent = x < 0.2 ? "near the clamp" : x > 0.8 ? "near the tip" : (x * 100).toFixed(0) + "% along";
    document.getElementById("fRead").innerHTML = "pitch change: <b>" + Math.abs(cents).toFixed(0) + " cents " + (cents < 0 ? "flatter" : "sharper") + "</b>";
  }
  fx.addEventListener("input", fRead);
  function blowAt(f) { C.play(fadeOut(C.render(C.toHz(C.models.harmonica.partials(), f), 1.3), 0.25), 0.6); }
  document.getElementById("fPlay").addEventListener("click", function () { blowAt(523.25 * ratio()); });
  document.getElementById("fOrig").addEventListener("click", function () { blowAt(523.25); });

  C.onTheme(hspec);
  relabel(); hspec(); fRead();
})();
</script>
```
